```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(AKCatchments)
options(AKCatchments.cache = file.path(tempdir(), "ak_vignette_cache"))
```

Every catchment attribute in this package is a summary of somebody else's
map or model over a polygon we drew. Both can be wrong. This vignette
covers what is common to all layers: how to read the uncertainty columns,
where error comes from, the central problem of aggregating map error to a
catchment, how the uncertainty reaches your observations, what it does to
analyses, and the alternatives at a glance. Each dataset's own
calculation is in its vignette (section 4 lists them). Chunks that only
compute are run, so the numbers below come from the package itself.

## 1. Reading the columns

| suffix | meaning | how to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `_se` | standard error: the SD of the plausible true values around the reported one | error bars, reliability, measurement-error models |
| `_lo95`, `_hi95` | 95% interval; may be asymmetric (bounded variables) | report with the value |
| `_lo`, `_hi` (soils, Pastick) | **bounds or ranges, not intervals**: the value under the most and least favourable assumption, or an average of the product's low/high values | sensitivity analyses, not error bars |
| `geol_major_contains_pct_*` / `geol_contains_pct_*` | lower and upper bounds of the same quantity | report both |
| `_flag` | named conditions under which the value should not be trusted as is | filter, stratify or report |
| `_coverage_pct` | share of the catchment the map covers; the value describes only that part | check before use |

An SE describes a distribution; a bound describes an assumption. Don't turn
bounds into SEs (dividing a range by 4 implies a distribution the product
never gave), and don't treat an SE as a bound.

## Computing the attributes

```{r usage, eval = FALSE}
x <- ak_catchments(pts) |>                                # or import_catchments(your polygons)
  ak_alder() |>                                           # each layer appends its value and uncertainty columns
  ak_landcover(error_matrix = em) |>                      # Olofsson adjustment when you have a matrix
  ak_permafrost(sigma_m = 1000) |>
  ak_soils(lh_range = 0.9)
w <- ak_weather(x, years = 1990:2023)
wx <- weather_at_samples(w, samples)                      # samples: site_code, sample_date
ak_layers(details = TRUE)                                 # product, citation, published error, method, assumptions
ak_provenance(x)                                          # where each column came from
attribute_reliability(x)                                  # how much of each variable's spread is error
```

## 2. Where uncertainty comes from

Every number has up to six sources of error. The columns carry some of them
and not others, and it matters which.

| code | source | example | who causes it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P** | the product is wrong | the alder map predicts 12% where there is 20% | the data producer |
| **A** | aggregating pixel errors to the catchment | whether 10,000 alder pixels' errors cancel or add up | our assumption about spatial correlation |
| **S** | sampling | Daymet averaged over 10-50 points, not every pixel | our calculation |
| **D** | delineation | the polygon includes a neighbour's headwater | our delineation |
| **T** | time mismatch | glacier outlines from about 2000, samples from 2020 | the product's date vs yours |
| **M** | method choices | permafrost class ranges, channel threshold, rain-snow ramp | our (documented) assumptions |

What each layer's uncertainty columns include:

| layer | function | P | A | S | D | T | M | kind of uncertainty reported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| polygon | `ak_catchments()`, `ak_delineate()` | – | – | – | flags, validation | – | flags | diagnostics, flags, IoU against references |
| topography | `ak_topography()` | – | – | – | – | – | resolution | values at 10 and 30 m; `topo_flag` |
| outlet slope | `ak_outlet_slope()` | – | – | – | snap | – | two reaches | sensitivity (100 vs 200 m) |
| alder | `ak_alder()` | yes | yes | – | – | – | – | SE, Beta 95% interval, flags |
| alder, WRST alternate | `ak_alder(source = "nps_wrst")` | signature spread | exact | – | – | – | unrecorded alder | SE, Beta 95% interval, unrecorded share, flags |
| land cover | `ak_landcover()` | with an error matrix | regional | – | – | – | – | bias-adjusted shares, SE, flags |
| permafrost (Jorgenson) | `ak_permafrost()` | class ranges, positions | yes | – | – | – | midpoints | simulated SE and 95% interval, flag |
| permafrost (Pastick) | `ak_permafrost(source = "pastick2015")` | – | – | – | – | – | masked land | bounds, flags |
| geology | `ak_geology()` | composition | – | – | – | – | equal allocation | bounds; optional positional spread |
| soils | `ak_soils()` | composition | – | – | – | – | L/H as 90% range | SE and interval for shares; L/H bounds |
| glaciers | `ak_glaciers()` | positions | yes | – | – | not included | – | simulated SE and 95% interval, flag |
| fire | `ak_fire*()` | detection threshold | – | – | – | – | – | threshold carried; flag |
| PRISM normals | `ak_climate_normals()` | – | – | – | – | – | – | consistency flag only |
| daily weather | `ak_weather()` | not included | – | yes | – | – | – | sampling SE, flag |
| weather anomalies | `weather_at_samples()` | not included | – | yes | – | – | – | sampling SE, flag |
| snow-off | `ak_snowoff()` | yes | – | – | – | – | conservative fill | SE per site-year, flags |
| degree days since snow-off | `weather_at_samples(snowoff = )` | via snow-off | – | – | – | – | – | delta-method SE |
| stream temperature, USGS | `ak_obs_*()` | provider QC | – | – | – | – | – | qualifiers carried |
| climate projections | `ak_climate_projection()`, `projection_ensemble()` | model spread | sub-grid flagged | internal variability | – | – | one run per model | per-model SE, ensemble SD and interval, flags |
| greenness | `ak_peak_ndvi()` | calibration | shared peak error | points | – | – | calibration floor | SE, 95% interval, trend SE with sensor steps, flags |

Two absences matter most. **Delineation error (D) is in no `_se`
column**: it is reported through flags and validation, and measured with
`polygon_spread()` (`vignette("delineation")`, section 6). **Daymet's
interpolation error (P) is not in the weather SEs**, because no Alaska
figures exist yet (`vignette("weather-daymet")`).

## 3. The core problem: aggregating map error to a catchment

Every cell of the catchment is summarised, so the catchment mean *of the
map* has no sampling error. Its error is the map's own error, averaged over
the catchment. How much averaging helps depends on how the errors of
neighbouring pixels are correlated:

- if pixel errors were independent, the SE of a mean over *n* pixels would
  be the pixel RMSE / √n: near zero for any real catchment;
- if they are fully correlated (the map is off by the same amount
  everywhere in the catchment), averaging doesn't help at all.

Map errors are strongly correlated: they come from model bias by
landscape type, scene effects and regional calibration. The ACCS alder map
shows it directly: its RMSE is 10.5% cover at a 10 m site, 4.9% over 10 x
10 km and 1.4% over an ecoregion (Nawrocki et al. 2021). With independent
errors the 10 x 10 km figure would be about 0.01%.

```{r alder-aggregation}
area <- c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000)                     # km2
data.frame(area_km2 = area,
           independent_pixels = round(10.5 / sqrt(area * 1e4), 3),   # 10 m pixels
           package = round(AKCatchments:::alder_se(area), 2),                    # interpolated on log(area)
           fully_correlated = 10.5)
```

The package's choice is the middle column: the published RMSE at each
scale, interpolated on log(area). Do not use the SD of the pixel values
inside the catchment, or a bootstrap of them, as an SE: that measures how
varied the catchment is, not how uncertain its mean is.

## 5. How the uncertainty reaches your observations

Water samples, invertebrate samples and other observations get catchment
attributes by joining: static attributes by site, time-varying ones by
site and date. The error comes along, and its **structure** matters as
much as its size.

| attribute | error shared by | examples |
|---|---|---|
| static attributes | every sample from the site | alder, land cover, permafrost, geology, soils, topography |
| polygon error | every attribute and every sample of the site | all of the above at once |
| snow-off, fire windows | every sample in the site-year | `snowoff_doy`, `days_since_snowoff`, `tdd_snowoff`, `burn_frac_5yr` |
| weather anomalies | samples on the same date (and nearby dates) | `t_anom7`, `p_anom30` |
| regional product bias | every site in a region | NLCD error matrix, alder ecoregion RMSE, Daymet station density, permafrost class ranges |

Consequences:

- **A site's samples are not independent replicates of its attributes.**
  Repeating a static value and its SE on 30 samples does not give 30
  pieces of information about the attribute. Keep static and time-varying
  tables separate (CAKN-Data does), and model the attribute's error at
  the site level.
- **Errors are correlated across attributes of a site** through the
  polygon, and within compositional sets (land-cover shares sum to 100).
- **Shared regional errors move whole regions.** They bias intercepts and
  between-region contrasts more than within-region slopes.

## 6. What the uncertainty does downstream

### Classical vs Berkson error

- *Classical*: observed = true + error (sampling error, a noisy
  measurement). Regression slopes on the observed value are attenuated
  toward zero by the reliability ratio λ = var(true) / var(observed).
- *Berkson*: true = observed + error (a smooth model prediction or a
  group average assigned to members). Slopes are not attenuated; only
  their uncertainty is understated.

Map products made by statistical models (alder cover, permafrost
probability, interpolated weather, PRISM) are closer to Berkson;
classification maps (NLCD, permafrost classes) misclassify, which is
neither; Daymet point sampling is classical. A quick simulation:

```{r berkson}
set.seed(2)
n <- 2000
true_c <- rnorm(n); obs_c <- true_c + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7)        # classical
obs_b <- rnorm(n); true_b <- obs_b + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7)         # Berkson
y_c <- 2 * true_c + rnorm(n); y_b <- 2 * true_b + rnorm(n)
c(true_slope = 2, classical = unname(coef(lm(y_c ~ obs_c))[2]), berkson = unname(coef(lm(y_b ~ obs_b))[2]),
  expected_classical = 2 / (1 + 0.7^2))
```

### How much does error matter for your variables?

`attribute_reliability()` compares each variable's SE with its spread across
sites. Reliability near 1 means the error is negligible for comparing
sites; near 0 means the values differ mostly by error:

```{r reliability}
x <- data.frame(site_code = letters[1:6],
                alnus_cover = c(1, 3, 8, 15, 30, 45), alnus_cover_se = c(6, 6, 5, 4.5, 4, 4),
                totperm_pct = c(55, 60, 62, 70, 75, 80), totperm_pct_se = c(12, 10, 11, 8, 9, 7))
attribute_reliability(x)
```

Here alder's error is small next to its range across sites, while the
permafrost values differ between sites by no more than their error
(reliability 0): a permafrost effect would be hard to detect and, under
classical error, its slope underestimated.

### Ways to use the columns, roughly in order of effort

1. **Report** values with their intervals and flags; that is what the
   columns are for.
2. **Screen**: run `attribute_reliability()`; drop or stratify by flags
   (`delin_ok`, `partial_coverage`, `jitter_dominates`,
   `small_catchment`) and check whether results change.
3. **Sensitivity**: refit with the `_lo` and `_hi` bounds, or with
   alternative assumptions (`sigma_m`, `lh_range`, `concentration`).
4. **Simulation**: draw plausible values per *site* (normal on a suitable
   scale, or Beta for percentages, using `_se`), refit for each draw, and
   combine the fits (multiple-imputation rules). Draw once per site and
   reuse the draw for all of the site's samples.
5. **Measurement-error models**: treat the true attribute as a latent
   variable at the site level. Note that `brms::me()` puts an independent
   error on each row; with several samples per site that is wrong for
   static attributes (it treats the site's error as independent across
   its samples). Model the site-level covariate in a separate part of the
   model, or aggregate to sites first.

The CAKN nitrogen analysis uses the columns as a data product (options 1-3)
and does not feed them into its models; other users may need 4 or 5.

## 7. Alternatives at a glance

| layer | package method | alternative | effect of switching |
|---|---|---|---|
| alder | RMSE interpolated on log(area) | fully correlated (site RMSE everywhere) | SEs 1.5-3x larger for 1-1000 km² |
| alder | Beta interval | logit delta method | absurdly wide intervals at low cover |
| alder (WRST) | unrecorded alder = class mean | unrecorded alder = 0 | lower alder where aerial plots dominate; SE unchanged |
| land cover | no adjustment unless a matrix is given | Olofsson with the 2001 matrix | shares shift systematically; SE added |
| permafrost | uniform within class, rigid shifts, σ = 1 km | central-weighted class fractions; per-boundary jitter; σ 0.5-2 km | smaller SE; smaller SE for large catchments; SE roughly scales with σ in small catchments |
| permafrost | isolated 1-10% | isolated 0-10% | midpoint 5.5 → 5%; tiny effect |
| geology | bounds; σ = 127 m if run | σ = 59 m (strict NMAS) or 2-4x | narrower or wider positional spread |
| soils | L/H as a 90% range | L/H as an 80% range | SE about 28% larger |
| soils | concentration 20 where L/H missing | 5 or 50 | much larger or smaller SE for those map units |
| Daymet | sampling SE only | add Alaska station cross-validation error | larger SE, mostly for absolute values, little for anomalies |
| Daymet | 10-50 sampled points | every pixel (gridded download) | no sampling error; more download |
| snow-off fill | conservative: RMSE² + s² + v | independent errors: s² − RMSE² + v | smaller SE for filled years |
| snow-off MODIS | regional RMSE | RMSE scaled by cloud days | larger SE in cloudy years |
| snow-off | MODIS + Daymet fill | passive-microwave snow-off (Pan et al. 2020; 6.25 km, not affected by cloud, about ±11 days) as an independent check | a between-product spread |
| polygon | flags, validation, alternative polygons | boundary jitter | misleadingly small, structural errors missed |
| climate projections | per-model deltas + ensemble spread | ensemble mean only | hides structural uncertainty |
| climate projections | prediction interval for one more model | model range (min-max) | narrower with few models |
| greenness | sensors calibrated to Landsat 7 | uncalibrated | sensor offsets of a few hundredths; spurious trends |
| greenness | peak SE shared among points | independent among points | SE several times smaller for large catchments |
| greenness | calibration SE floor 0.002 | held-out bias only | smaller trend SE |

## 8. What is not included, and what would close the gaps

- Delineation error in the `_se` columns: use `polygon_spread()`.
- Daymet interpolation error: needs the Daymet V4 station
  cross-validation files for Alaska (ORNL DAAC).
- NLCD 2016 accuracy: needs the Selkowitz and Stehman (2011) error matrix
  or your own reference points.
- Map dates against sample dates (glaciers ~2000, NLCD 2016, Jorgenson
  ~2008, alder ~2010s): flagged in the documentation, not quantified.
- PRISM and Pastick: no error distribution published; bounds and flags
  only.
- Soil map-unit and geology contact positions: optional, through
  `positional_uncertainty()`.
